Problem

Problem

Brand partnerships needed deeper retailer insights

Badho wanted to partner with smaller FMCG brands to grow monetisation. Brands were interested, but they needed store-level insights about retailers that profiles didn’t capture yet.

  1. GapPersonas were a blind spotLittle data to personalise the app
  3. GoalDeep retailer insightsBrand-targeted adsPersonalised UX
  5. SoCollect it through the retailer profileBusiness + persona data
How I scoped it 1Met brand onboarding → 2Listed the data needed

Audit

The old profile was an MVP, and barely used

Few retailers ever reached it, and the ones who did rarely filled anything in.

  1. 1

    Entry point buried in the side drawer

    Only reachable via hamburger menu → Profile. For kirana owners using the app daily, it was effectively invisible.

  2. 2

    No progress, no motivation

    Users couldn’t see how complete their profile was, what was missing, or what they’d gain by filling it in.

  3. 3

    40–50% of the screen was blank

    Almost nothing above the fold: no data, no sense of progress, no reason to engage.

Objectives

What we set out to do

  • Increase profile views

    Make the profile visible in the app, ideally reachable from Home.

  • More shop photos and shop data

    To understand each retailer’s shop type and products.

How might we

How might we motivate retailers to complete their profiles?

In a way that feels natural, not forced.
Barrier 1 · Discoverability

Invisible in the app

☰ Menu→Side drawer→Profile

The profile sat behind the menu and side drawer, outside the daily purchase flow.

Barrier 2 · Motivation

No reason to fill it in

No progress, no visible benefit, no hint of what was missing. For busy retailers, no payoff meant no effort.

Decisions

Key decision

The biggest barrier wasn’t motivation, it was discoverability

So we changed where the profile lives.

What changed in the side drawer

  1. 1Upload shop photos straight from the drawer, so they get more visibility
  2. 2A profile progress bar

Scope kept tightNothing else changed, to avoid dev effort on new components.

Why this mattered

  1. 1Profile was buried in the side drawer, hard to find and harder to revisit
  2. 2A bottom-nav tab gives it permanent visibility, so completing the profile becomes part of daily use, not a hidden task

Scope kept tightNothing else changed, to avoid dev effort on new components.

Trade-off

Discoverability over familiarity

  1. Why Order Now was replaced

    Analytics showed Order Now had the lowest engagement in the bottom nav, so it was the best slot to replace.

  2. The cost: relearning the nav

    Users already knew the old nav. Moving it meant short-term learning effort, but the long-term gain outweighed it.

  3. The payoff: richer retailer profiles

    Richer profiles directly support KYC, customer segmentation and future brand initiatives.

Decision stories

Where I had to convince

Three calls I argued for, and where we landed.

1

Adding a shareable business card

Evidence
PL

Product Lead Their argument

Keep the profile about data collection. A generated card adds design, share and download work to V1.

P

Me My counter

The old profile gave retailers no reason to fill it in. A business card is an instant payoff: add your shop details, get a card to share on WhatsApp or download. Every share also markets Badho.

How we landed

Shipped in Badho’s brand colours, as one fixed layout with Share and Download. Every state is designed, so the card is never empty.

In one lineLeads saw extra scope. I showed it was the payoff that gets profiles filled, and every share markets Badho.

2

Dropping badges, motivating through copy

Evidence
→
Copy on screen
  • “Dukan ke photos ke bina aapki dukan ki pehchaan adhoori hai”
  • “More shop photos = More trust & better brand, seller matches!”
  • “Verify your profile to receive monthly payouts and brand schemes”
  • “Share your landmark and get product ideas based on the people around your shop”
DV

Dev / APM Their argument

Badges need high tech effort for this release.

P

Me My counter

Badges were one route to motivation, not the goal. Retailers act when they see what’s in it for them. So I wrote the payoff into every prompt, in simple Hinglish, right where we ask them to act.

How we landed

No badges. Copy, a progress bar and a Complete Profile button carry the motivation, at no extra build cost.

In one lineBadges cost too much to build, so the motivation moved into the copy: every prompt says what the retailer gets.

3

Making KYC hard to miss

Evidence
→
ST

Stakeholders V2 feedback

KYC has low emphasis. It needs to stand out.

P

Me My counter

KYC felt like an admin chore, so it got skipped. I tied it to the payoff already in the copy, monthly payouts and brand schemes, and made it a clear card with a Verify button.

How we landed

A high-emphasis KYC nudge with pending, in-review and resubmit states.

In one lineV2 hid KYC, so I made it a benefit card with a button and states.

Learnings

Reflection

What I learned, and what I’d do next

Learnings

  1. 01

    Value communication is a multiplier

    Retailers filled in fields once they saw the payoff (better schemes, brand offers). Nudges alone did less.

  2. 02

    Profile data opened a new B2B revenue stream

    Rich store data let FMCG brands target specific retailers, creating a new partnership and ad channel for Badho.

  3. 03

    The profile is a data gold mine

    Better segmentation shows each retailer’s preferences, environment and goals, the base for detailed persona analysis.

What I’d improve

  1. 01

    Track business card shares and downloads

    To measure adoption properly.

  2. 02

    Design for new sections

    A section added later got far fewer submissions than the others.

  3. 03

    Analyse the user journey

    Which sections go unfilled, and why. Photos got more submissions than text fields.
